item.title: Project under fire
item.description: COMMUNITY leaders in the Malomalo district are demanding greater transparency over the proposed Google Data Center at Natadola Beach, claiming the project proceeded without adequate consultation on its long-term environmental impacts. Malomalo district representative Emoni Rokomoce said residents remained concerned about the lack of engagement and the potential impact on marine resources.
item.content:encoded:
COMMUNITY leaders in the Malomalo district are demanding greater transparency over the proposed Google Data Center at Natadola Beach, claiming the project proceeded without adequate consultation on its long-term environmental impacts.

Malomalo district representative Emoni Rokomoce said residents remained concerned about the lack of engagement and the potential impact on marine resources.

“On the beach there are red and white cords tied to cables which run underground right up to where the construction works are taking place,” he said.

“Our concern is how this will impact our natural resources, especially the sea and the marine life.”

Mr Rokomoce also accused the developers of using dishonest processes to secure the site.

Nadroga Navosa Resource Owners Committee representative Mosese Volavola said legal action could be considered, claiming landowners were not fully informed about the project’s scope.

“FNPF is at fault because they were not clear about the other activities that would go on once the project was up and running and the landowners were not consulted,” he said.

“They were only to lease the land. Once they touched the qoliqoli, they should have gotten approval. The resource owners’ understanding was that this was a tourism lease.”

The iTaukei Land Trust Board (TLTB) confirmed it granted a 25-year sublease to Natadola Bay Resort Ltd (FNPF) from January 1, 2025, which was later assigned to Staghorn Services Pte Ltd for the Google Data Center and registered on February 23, 2026.

TLTB said two consultation meetings were held with FNPF and affected landowners in May and July 2025 at Sanasana Village, where the project and premium payments were discussed. However, it said its consultation responsibility was limited to the affected landowning unit and Sanasana Village, while wider community engagement fell under the Ministry of Lands and the Provincial Office.

Questions sent last week to FNPF, Google, Energy Fiji Limited and the Water Authority of Fiji remained unanswered.

item.title: Call to address grievances
item.description: THE legacy of more than 30 laws introduced under the previous government continues to undermine iTaukei rights and institutions, according to Roko Tui Dreketi Ro Teimumu Kepa, who is calling for those grievances to be addressed before Fiji can move forward on questions of national identity. item.content:encoded:
THE legacy of more than 30 laws introduced under the previous government continues to undermine iTaukei rights and institutions, according to Roko Tui Dreketi Ro Teimumu Kepa, who is calling for those grievances to be addressed before Fiji can move forward on questions of national identity.

Speaking after the Rewa Provincial Council meeting last week, Ro Teimumu said the former administration’s 16-year rule caused lasting damage to indigenous institutions, arguing that key legislation targeting the iTaukei community remained unresolved.

“What they did was they took right from the top and I think over 30 pieces of legislation targeting us iTaukei,” she said.

Ro Teimumu said discussions on the identity of Fijians could not be separated from what she described as the erosion of indigenous rights and institutions.

She pointed to the abolition of the Great Council of Chiefs (GCC) under the 2007 decree as one of the most significant decisions affecting the iTaukei, saying it dismantled an institution that had played a central role in Fiji’s history.

“Those are the issues that need to be addressed first.”

Ro Teimumu also criticised the 2013 Constitution, claiming it had affected matters central to indigenous communities, including customary land ownership and traditional fishing grounds.

“That is our land, our qoliqoli, and gave us the heart of our discussions today.”

She warned that unresolved issues surrounding indigenous rights would continue to affect future generations if they were not addressed.

item.title: Dass urges inclusive dialogue
item.description: ANY potential sale of the Fiji Sugar Corporation to a private entity must involve widespread industry consultation, says Lautoka Cane Producers Association chairman Bala Dass. Responding to recent comments by Prime Minister Sitiveni Rabuka regarding privatisation discussions, Mr Dass said a decision of this magnitude cannot be made by the Government alone.
item.content:encoded:
ANY potential sale of the Fiji Sugar Corporation to a private entity must involve widespread industry consultation, says Lautoka Cane Producers Association chairman Bala Dass.

Responding to recent comments by Prime Minister Sitiveni Rabuka regarding privatisation discussions, Mr Dass said a decision of this magnitude cannot be made by the Government alone.

“The Prime Minister himself cannot make the decision to sell this because there are so many people involved in it,” he said.

“The farmers are involved, the labourers are involved, the truck drivers are involved, the FSC employees are involved,that is something that has to be consulted.”

Mr Dass warned that transitioning the corporation to private ownership would require extensive negotiation to protect stakeholders and ensure continued state support.

“If it is owned by a private company, then a lot of things need to be negotiated, and what we want is the government’s involvement.”

Mr Dass called on Government leadership to provide full transparency on what privatisation would entail for the industry.

“The Government has to somehow or other, whether it is a private company, whether it is a statutory body or whatever, have some say on it because people are involved.

” A large number of people, about 20 per cent of the population of this country, is involved in the industry. It is not that easy for the government to sell the whole thing to somebody else.

“We also need expertise to advise on it.”

item.title: Lal calls for youth participation in national talks
item.description: FIJI needs young people who can engage in meaningful discussions, challenge misinformation and contribute responsibly to national conversations, says Dialogue Fiji executive director Nilesh Lal. Speaking at the Fiji National University (FNU) Inter-Division Debate Competition 2026 at the Valelevu Campus on Saturday, Mr Lal said critical thinking and respectful dialogue were essential pillars of a s
item.content:encoded:
FIJI needs young people who can engage in meaningful discussions, challenge misinformation and contribute responsibly to national conversations, says Dialogue Fiji executive director Nilesh Lal.

Speaking at the Fiji National University (FNU) Inter-Division Debate Competition 2026 at the Valelevu Campus on Saturday, Mr Lal said critical thinking and respectful dialogue were essential pillars of a strong democracy.

He said democracy depended on citizens who were able to analyse information, consider different perspectives and participate constructively in public discussions.

“Democracy depends on citizens who can think critically, distinguish evidence from misinformation and participate constructively in public discussion,” he said.

Mr Lal said democratic participation required people to engage with differing views without hostility while remaining open to reconsidering their positions when presented with stronger evidence.

He said the growing influence of social media had made these skills even more important, as public discussions were increasingly shaped by simplified arguments and emotional reactions.

“In an age of social media, where complex issues are often reduced to slogans, insults and emotionally charged claims, these qualities are more important than ever.”

Mr Lal said young people had a critical role in shaping Fiji’s future by bringing greater honesty, depth and responsibility to national conversations.

“Fiji needs young people who can bring greater depth, honesty and responsibility into our national conversations.”

He encouraged students taking part in the debate competition to use their voices responsibly and continue developing the skills needed to strengthen democratic participation.

item.title: Act on risks, PRB urged
item.description: THE Public Rental Board (PRB) should be responsible for ensuring condemned buildings are secured and no longer occupied, a parliamentary committee has heard. The issue was raised last Friday during submissions by the National Fire Authority (NFA) to the Parliamentary Standing Committee on Social Affairs on the Public Health (Amendment) Bill 2026.
item.content:encoded:
THE Public Rental Board (PRB) should be responsible for ensuring condemned buildings are secured and no longer occupied, a parliamentary committee has heard.

The issue was raised last Friday during submissions by the National Fire Authority (NFA) to the Parliamentary Standing Committee on Social Affairs on the Public Health (Amendment) Bill 2026.

Opposition MP Ketan Lal questioned what role public health authorities would play in dealing with unsafe structures, citing the condemned PRB flats in Nabua where people continued to enter and occupy the buildings.

“You can still see people hanging around that place,” Mr Lal said.

“It’s unsafe. According to engineers, it’s unsafe. So how will the public health board step in?”

Responding, Ministry of Health WASH coordinator Toga Vosataki said the matter primarily fell under the National Fire Authority’s jurisdiction.

“In that particular case, since the building is clearly in the jurisdiction of NFA, NFA will take lead in not only conducting the investigation but ensuring that it’s cordoned off in such a way that no one can actually come in and start to squat or stay within the facility,” Mr Vosataki said.

He added that the NFA could seek police assistance to remove occupants, while public health authorities would only intervene where occupied dwellings posed a direct health risk.

Government MP Praveen Kumar then questioned who would be liable if a condemned building remained occupied and an accident occurred before demolition.

Mr Vosataki said responsibility rested with the PRB as the owner of the structure.

“I believe that the team from National Fire Authority would agree with me, for that particular scenario, the PRB will be responsible since the structure is theirs, and they should have a plan in place to demolish or repurpose that particular structure,” he said.

He said the PRB should also coordinate with police to prevent people from entering buildings at risk of collapse.

item.title: NFA seeks demolition checks
item.description: THE National Fire Authority (NFA) is calling for mandatory consultation before unsafe buildings are demolished, warning that premature demolition could destroy critical evidence needed for fire investigations. Making a submission to the Parliamentary Standing Committee on Social Affairs on the Public Health (Amendment) Bill 2026 last Friday, NFA chief executive officer Sowane Puamau said the autho
item.content:encoded:
THE National Fire Authority (NFA) is calling for mandatory consultation before unsafe buildings are demolished, warning that premature demolition could destroy critical evidence needed for fire investigations.

Making a submission to the Parliamentary Standing Committee on Social Affairs on the Public Health (Amendment) Bill 2026 last Friday, NFA chief executive officer Sowane Puamau said the authority was seeking a simple requirement for the Ministry of Health to consult the NFA before ordering the demolition of properties affected by fire.

“The reason why we are bringing this up is so that we don’t mess up with all these things, like the Public Health saying, ‘Destroy that thing’ without consulting us. We have already completed our investigation on that,” Mr Puamau said.

“It’s just a simple consultation with us, just stating that yes, you can go ahead because we’ve already completed our report and it’s already in.”

He said the proposed measure would ensure the NFA was able to carry out its statutory responsibility of determining the cause of fires before evidence was destroyed.

“They cannot order demolition without consulting us, and if we haven’t completed the investigation,” he said.

Mr Puamau acknowledged that some damaged buildings might pose public health risks, but stressed that due process must still be followed.

He added that people could be held accountable if evidence was destroyed before the NFA completed its investigations, underscoring the importance of preserving fire scenes until investigators had finished their work.

item.title: inDepth I Hidden school crisis
item.description: FOR generations, Fiji’s schools have been regarded as safe spaces where children learn, grow and prepare for adulthood. Today, however, educators are confronting a challenge that extends far beyond textbooks and examinations. Drugs, risky behaviour and a rapidly escalating HIV epidemic among young people are forcing schools to take on an increasingly important role in protecting students — not onl
item.content:encoded:
FOR generations, Fiji’s schools have been regarded as safe spaces where children learn, grow and prepare for adulthood. Today, however, educators are confronting a challenge that extends far beyond textbooks and examinations.

Drugs, risky behaviour and a rapidly escalating HIV epidemic among young people are forcing schools to take on an increasingly important role in protecting students — not only from academic failure, but from life-threatening health risks.

That stark reality was laid bare during the School Management Association of Fiji conference in Suva, where National Substance Abuse Advisory Council (NSAAC) acting chief executive Josua Naisele urged school leaders to recognise that they are now on the frontline of one of Fiji’s biggest public health crises.

“This is happening in our schools now,” Mr Naisele told delegates.

“Teachers are on the front line of early detection and referral.”

His presentation painted a picture that was both alarming and urgent.

By the end of 2025, Fiji had recorded 5676 cumulative HIV cases, including 2016 new infections in a single year.

The epidemic is increasingly affecting young people, with HIV cases among children aged 10 to 14 increasing by 892 per cent since 2015 and infections among 15 to 19-year-olds surging by an astonishing 4183 per cent.

The largest number of new infections is now among people aged 20 to 24, while those under 25 account for 58 per cent of all new HIV cases recorded last year.

For school leaders gathered at the conference, those statistics carried a sobering message: the HIV epidemic is no longer something happening elsewhere.

It is affecting students, families and communities connected to Fiji’s schools.

Mr Naisele explained that the country’s drug problem and HIV epidemic are becoming increasingly intertwined.

“Injection drug use is the number one identified HIV transmission route,” he said.

The presentation showed that injecting drug use accounted for 18 per cent of all new HIV infections recorded in Fiji during 2025, with the overlap between injecting drug use and sexual transmission continuing to grow.

Needle sharing remains one of the most efficient ways HIV spreads.

“When people inject drugs and share needles, HIV passes directly through blood. Even microscopic blood residue is enough.”

Mr Naisele also warned that alcohol and drugs impaired judgement, making young people more likely to engage in unprotected sex, accept dangerous risks or become victims of exploitation.

Drug dependence, he said, could also drive vulnerable young people into transactional or survival sex, exposing them not only to HIV but also to sexually transmitted infections, violence and poor access to healthcare.

While methamphetamine has dominated national headlines, Mr Naisele said schools continue to face a range of substance abuse issues.

Cannabis remains the most common drug used by school-age children and is often the first drug they experiment with before progressing to harder substances.

Alcohol is widely accessible and frequently linked to sexual risk-taking and violence during school events and weekends.

Inhalants such as glue and petrol continue to be used by younger secondary and upper primary students, causing serious damage to developing brains while remaining difficult to detect.

Methamphetamine, meanwhile, is emerging rapidly, with injecting already reported among school-age users in Suva through older drug networks.

The presentation also highlighted growing concerns about sexting and online exploitation, noting that young people using drugs face greater risks of sexual exploitation and transactional sex.

Mr Naisele said substance abuse rarely occurred in isolation.

Peer pressure, the desire to fit in, family dysfunction, trauma, abuse, poverty, lack of awareness about HIV, stigma surrounding help-seeking and limited adult supervision all combined to increase children’s vulnerability.

These factors often reinforce one another, creating environments where experimentation can quickly develop into addiction and risky behaviour.

The challenge, he suggested, cannot be solved through enforcement alone.

He said it requires stronger families, better-informed communities and schools that recognise problems before they escalate.

One of the strongest messages from the presentation was that teachers are not expected to become doctors or investigators.

item.title: Court to set meth trial date
item.description: THE High Court in Suva will set a trial date for two police officers and two civilians charged with methamphetamine-related offences when the matter is recalled in three months. Police officers Sevuloni Lubi, 43, and Ratu Lote Lewaivanua, 32, together with civilians Eroni Kitanamati Bati, 37, and Alipate Matadigo, appeared before Justice Daniel Goundar for a pre-trial conference last Friday.
item.content:encoded:
THE High Court in Suva will set a trial date for two police officers and two civilians charged with methamphetamine-related offences when the matter is recalled in three months.

Police officers Sevuloni Lubi, 43, and Ratu Lote Lewaivanua, 32, together with civilians Eroni Kitanamati Bati, 37, and Alipate Matadigo, appeared before Justice Daniel Goundar for a pre-trial conference last Friday.

The four are charged in relation to the alleged importation and possession of 4.7 kilograms of liquid methamphetamine in 2025.

Justice Goundar directed the men’s lawyers to resolve all outstanding litigation issues, including any representations relating to the charges, before the matter is recalled on November 6.

Senior State lawyer Eoghn Samisoni informed the court that the prosecution would not rely on the accused men’s caution interviews at trial because they contained no admissions.

Sevuloni Lubi outside the High Court in Suva on Friday.
